source_text: Sensus est igitur concupiscentia, et mala qualitas non est; ergo quando minuitur concupiscentia, sensus minuitur claudens - ut loqueris - Aristotelis palaestram, ut inde ad sacras Litteras revertaris
pass_a_gloss: Sensus is therefore desire, and evils qualitas not is; therefore when minuitur desire, sensus minuitur claudens - so-that/as loqueris - of-Aristotle palaestram, so-that/as from-there to sacras Litteras revertaris.

lemmas.lexica: LS concupiscentia=eager desire; Blaise Christian usage often sexual desire vs nuptiae
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Closing Aristotle’s wrestling school, let us return from it to the sacred Scriptures.
Sexual desire, then, is a sensation, and it is not an evil quality. Therefore, when sexual desire is diminished, sensation is diminished.

choices.why: Julian distinguishes nuptiae from concupiscentia; do not flatten to 'lust' as a nature-sin substance.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded. Julian is not first-English.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Contra Iulianum / Against Julian), including authorities Julian quoted; Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
